overview: Two studies used noninvasive stimulation to test causal roles in memory: [beta-frequency rTMS over the right angular gyrus](#p2) improved the precision of temporal memory for movie clips, with the benefit on low-confidence trials, and [transcranial ultrasound to the hippocampus](#p5) impaired inference based on relational structure. A second thread is that processing and its apparent consequences can come apart. [People who mentally manipulated water in opaque cups](#p0) often failed to notice it was gone, and [readers' eye movements during mind-wandering](#p6) still tracked word frequency, length and surprisal even as comprehension fell. On aging, [adults in their 70s and 80s accessing word meanings faster than young adults](#p3) was traced to conceptual representations shaped by accumulated language experience. Two other results were more targeted: [a test of a secondary motor integration account of confidence](#p1) found no support for it, and [work on task-set inertia in dual tasking](#p4) showed that both local and global context affect how sticky task sets are. Finally, [a card game where players coordinate only through timing](#p7) found that humans adapted to their partners over the game while the AI models did

papers.title: You process it, yet miss the change: a magic-based demonstration of a novel form of change blindness
papers.authors: Cyril Thomas, André Didierjean
papers.summary: Forty participants mentally manipulated the water in opaque cups as part of an insight problem, and later the cups were turned upside down with no spill, thanks to a hidden superabsorbent powder. Most people showed no spontaneous surprise, and a good number later admitted they hadn't noticed the water was gone, even though they had actively thought about it and seen both the before and after states. It's a neat magic-trick route to a form of change blindness where the pre-change information was fully processed, and the authors link it to event boundaries.
papers.abstract: Previous research on change blindness has demonstrated that perceptual changes can sometimes go undetected despite preserved access to pre-change information. In the present study, we investigated whether change blindness can occur even when pre-change information is consciously and actively processed. Participants (N = 40) observed opaque cups filled with water (pre-change information) while mentally manipulating the liquid as part of an insight problem-solving task. After a memory digit-span task, the cups were turned upside down without any liquid spilling (post-change information). This magic trick relied on superabsorbent powder secretly placed in the cups beforehand. Strikingly, most participants did not spontaneously report surprise, and subsequent reports (e.g., explicitly acknowledging that they had failed to notice the water's disappearance) provided more direct evidence of change blindness for a substantial subset. This occurred despite participants having actively processed the initial state of the cups and encoded both the pre- and post-change information. These findings highlight fundamental limits in adults' ability to monitor the coherence of their environment. We discuss the mechanisms underlying this novel form of change blindness, notably in relation to the phenomenon of event boundaries.

papers.title: Testing a secondary motor integration account of confidence computation
papers.authors: Axel Garnier-Allain, Vincent de Gardelle, Thibault Gajdos Preuss et al.
papers.summary: Confidence in a decision seems to be influenced by action-related cues, and one idea is that a secondary motor-level filter, which slows and sharpens responses, drives this. The researchers manipulated sensory noise and speed-accuracy instructions to see if stronger filtering would dampen the usual boost in confidence from noise, and found strong evidence that it didn't. Modeling showed the predicted dampening would be tiny anyway, and that this motor account did no better than plain evidence accumulation, so confidence doesn't need to be computed from motor integration.
papers.abstract: A growing body of empirical evidence suggests that confidence judgments are modulated by action-related cues, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Recent decision-making models propose that the evidence accumulation variable is continuously transmitted to the motor system, allowing motor plans to evolve in parallel with decision formation. At the motor level, a secondary leaky integration process acts as a filter that regulates the speed-accuracy tradeoff: the stronger the filter, the slower and more accurate the responses. Here, we tested whether action-related effects on confidence are mediated by this secondary motor integration process. We manipulated sensory noise using a doubly stochastic random dot motion task and varied the motor-level filter via speed-accuracy instructions. We reasoned that the positive effect of sensory noise on confidence observed in previous studies should be attenuated by stronger filtering in the accuracy condition compared to the speed condition. However, we found strong empirical evidence against this qualitative prediction. Computational modeling further revealed that the predicted attenuation was extremely small and that confidence predictions based on secondary motor integration offered no advantage over those based on evidence accumulation. Together, these results show that confidence need not be computed from secondary motor integration to account for the observed pattern.

papers.title: Beta-frequency rTMS over the right angular gyrus selectively enhances temporal memory precision for complex naturalistic events
papers.authors: Matteo Frisoni, Paolo Capotosto, Carlo Sestieri
papers.summary: A day after people watched a full-length movie, the researchers zapped the right angular gyrus with 20 Hz rTMS while they placed 2-second clips on a timeline of the film, using the vertex as a control site. Stimulation improved the precision of their temporal estimates but not performance on a matched number line task. The benefit showed up on low-confidence trials, which hints that this region helps with weaker memory traces and gives causal support for its role in placing memories in time.
papers.abstract: Neuroimaging studies point to the role of right posterior parietal regions, particularly the angular gyrus (AG), in retrieving the temporal context of events. However, their causal contribution to memory for the temporal structure of complex, naturalistic events remains unclear. Here, we applied 20 Hz repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) over the right AG during the retrieval of temporal information to test its causal role in temporal memory precision. Twenty-four hours after encoding a full-length movie, participants (N=24) completed a Timeline task, estimating the time of occurrence of 2-second video clips along a visual analogue scale (VAS) representing the movie's duration, and a matched Number Line control task. In a within-subjects design, stimulation was delivered at stimulus onset on each trial, with the vertex serving as the control site. Relative to vertex stimulation, 20 Hz rTMS over the right AG significantly improved temporal precision in the Timeline task, with no equivalent effect in the control task. Although overall confidence calibration was unaffected by the stimulation, the benefit was selective for low-confidence trials, suggesting a role for this region for weak mnemonic traces. These findings provide causal evidence of the right AG's contribution to the precision of temporal memory for naturalistic events. This extends our understanding of the cortical network that supports our ability to locate human memories in time.

papers.title: Older yet faster: Representational development explains accelerated semantic processing in older adults.
papers.authors: Ying Li, Wenjia Joyce Zhao, Shenghua Luan et al.
papers.summary: Older adults are often slower, but across three studies, people aged 70-80 were actually faster than 18-25 year olds at accessing word meanings. The team traced this to differences in older adults' conceptual representations, and simulations showed that such differences can emerge naturally from accumulated language experience. The advantage shrank when learned representations clashed with task demands, which supports a view of aging as lifelong learning with both gains and costs rather than just decline.
papers.abstract: Slower responses in older age are often taken as evidence for cognitive decline, yet they may also stem from representational changes shaped by lifelong learning. Building on the information-accumulation perspective on aging, we argue that behavioral change across the lifespan can arise from representational systems continuously updated through learning from the environment. This view predicts that aging may bring both benefits and costs: Performance improves when task demands are congruent with accumulated knowledge but declines when they conflict. We provide convergent evidence for this account across three studies, each comprising the following components. First, in tasks requiring participants to access word meanings (i.e., when task demands were congruent with representation), we found that older adults (70-80 years old) exhibited faster semantic processing speed than younger adults (18-25 years old), a finding that cannot be explained by decline-based accounts. Second, we traced this processing advantage to systematic changes in older adults' conceptual representations inferred from semantic rating tasks. Third, using learning simulation models, we demonstrated how such representational changes could emerge naturally from cumulative language experience. Replications across different samples, task requirements, and word stimuli strengthen the robustness of these findings. Finally, we identified a boundary condition: When learned representations contain information incongruent with task demands, older adults' greater learning experience not only attenuates their representational changes but also reduces processing-speed advantage. Altogether, our research challenges the explanatory framework of cognitive aging that emphasizes decline and compensation, advancing a more balanced view grounded in representational development and lifelong learning. papers.title: How global and local task contexts influence task-set inertia in dual tasking.
papers.authors: Anton Koger, Denise Nadine Stephan, Leif Johannsen et al.
papers.summary: Using a dual-task setup, this work looked at task-set inertia, where a task that's no longer relevant keeps interfering. Even on trials where people could ignore the memory task, a leftover cost of short delays between tasks remained, though it was smaller. It was bigger after a trial where they'd had to report, nearly vanished in predictable ignore blocks, and was larger in blocks that were mostly report trials, so both local and global context shape how sticky task sets are.
papers.abstract: Cognitive control must be flexibly adjusted when task demands change, yet task-set inertia can impair performance by keeping previously relevant task sets active. This study investigated task-set inertia using a hybrid psychological refractory period paradigm, combining a visual-vocal short-term memory task with an auditory-manual reaction time task. We manipulated the stimulus-onset asynchrony (SOA: 100 vs. 1,000 ms) and the relevance of the visual-vocal short-term memory task (task load: report the stimulus vs. ignore the stimulus). In Experiment 1, task load varied unpredictably (trial by trial) or predictably (in blocks). In Experiment 2, we implemented blocks with majority report or majority ignore trials (75% respectively) to examine how global task context influences task-set inertia. Results showed the expected SOA effect in report conditions, with worse performance in the auditory-manual reaction time task at short compared with long SOA. This SOA effect suggests a processing bottleneck between short-term memory consolidation of the visual target and response selection for the auditory target. The SOA effect persisted (but was smaller) in ignore trials, indicating task-set inertia. This residual SOA effect was modulated by the previous trials' task load, with a larger SOA effect when the previous trial was a report compared with an ignore trial. Additionally, the residual SOA effect almost disappeared in predictable ignore blocks and was modulated by the proportion manipulation, showing a larger SOA effect in majority report blocks. These findings show that both global and local task contexts influence task-set inertia, demonstrating that task sets are context sensitive and show involuntary persistence. papers.title: Causal role of human hippocampus in relational structure learning and inference
papers.authors: Deng Pan, Simone D’Ambrogio, Naomi Kingston et al.
papers.summary: Participants used what they already knew about relational structures to infer new relationships in a changing environment, and fMRI showed consistent representations of that structure in the hippocampus. Neural network simulations predicted what would happen if those representations were disrupted, and transcranial ultrasound to the hippocampus in a separate group of 20 people did impair structure-based inference. That gives causal evidence for the hippocampus in learning and using relational structure.
papers.abstract: When meeting new individuals or known individuals in new circumstances, we intuitively map out their relationships—not merely through direct experience, but by inferring new connections on the basis of prior relational knowledge. How such relational knowledge is represented and used in the brain remains a long-standing question in cognitive neuroscience. Here, using a behavioural task and computational modelling, we show that participants ( N = 36) leveraged existing knowledge of relational structures to infer new relationships, facilitating adaptation in changing environments. Whole-brain neuroimaging identified consistent representations of relational structure in the hippocampus. To investigate the causal link between hippocampal representations and inference, we used neural network simulations to predict the behavioural effects of disrupting such representations. Consistent with this prediction, transcranial ultrasound stimulation of the human hippocampus ( N = 20), transiently modulating its activity, disrupted structure-based inference ( P < 0.001, Cohen’s d = −0.89, 95% confidence interval −1.41 to −0.36), providing empirical evidence for a causal role of hippocampus in relational-structure learning and structure-based inference.

papers.title: Mind-wandering preserves word-level coupling while disrupting comprehension
papers.authors: Anirudh Natarajan, Paul Sajda
papers.summary: Using public eye-tracking and EEG data from 44 adults reading articles and flagging their own mind-wandering lapses, the researchers checked whether word properties still steered the eyes during lapses. Word frequency, length and surprisal still predicted skipping and gaze duration about as well as in normal reading, yet comprehension dropped sharply when lapses covered the sentences needed for later questions, and the fixation-related EEG response was smaller. So the eyes can keep following words while the reader isn't building a useful representation of the text.
papers.abstract: Readers can move their eyes through a page but retain little of its meaning when their minds wander. We tested whether word properties still guide their eyes during these lapses. We analyzed public eye-tracking and electroencephalography (EEG) data from 44 adults who read articles. They marked the text read during each lapse they noticed. We linked these spans to the sentences needed for later comprehension questions. Word frequency, length and surprisal still predicted which words readers skipped and how long they looked at them. Compared with on-task reading, these effects met equivalence bounds of $\pm$10% for skipping and $\pm$20% for gaze duration. Readers spent 14.6% longer on words during lapses. Yet readers answered less accurately when lapses covered sentences needed for a later question. The adjusted difference was 25.7 percentage points for lapses covering all versus none of these sentences. The fixation-related EEG response was 42.7% smaller during lapses. At left posterior-lateral sensor P7, the median increase in alpha power was 10.0%. Occipital sensor Oz showed no reliable increase. These results suggest that word properties can guide the eyes while readers fail to form or retain a useful representation of the text.

papers.title: Rational Use of Time for Social Coordination in Humans and AI
papers.authors: Xiulin Yang, Sirisha Gudavalli, Jennifer Hu
papers.summary: The Mind is a card game where players can't talk and can only coordinate through timing, which makes it a good test of how people use time as a social signal. Across 150 humans and several AI models, including computer-use agents and text-prompted LLMs, behavior was best described by a Bayesian strategy that infers a partner's beliefs from their timing. The difference is that humans adapted to their partners over the game while the models didn't, suggesting such reasoning can arise without real-time experience but that AI still struggles to adapt to implicit signals.
papers.abstract: All social interactions are situated in time. Previous studies have shown that humans are able to use implicit temporal cues, such as the duration of a pause, to infer others' mental states. But how do humans use temporal cues for dynamic, fine-grained social coordination? And can AI systems do the same, without ``experiencing'' continuous real-time as humans do? We study these questions using a cooperative card game task called The Mind, which requires players to achieve a shared goal across repeated interactions but forbids explicit communication: the only available signal is the passage of time. We evaluate 150 humans, and two classes of AI models which reflect different ways of operationalizing time in artificial systems: computer-use agents (CUAs), and standard text-prompted LLMs. We find that human behavior is best captured by a Bayesian strategy that infers a partner's belief from their timing---and similarly for frontier models. However, unlike humans, none of the tested models seem to efficiently adapt their behaviors to their partners' over the course of the game. From a cognitive perspective, our findings suggest that humans perform implicit probabilistic reasoning about continuous-time signals in dynamic social settings, and that such reasoning mechanisms may emerge without real-time experience. Practically, our study highlights new challenges for AI systems to coordinate efficiently with other agents by learning to interpret and adapt to their implicit signals in dynamic settings.

papers.title: Dorsolateral Prefrontal Cortex Causally Supports the Memory Advantage of Reading Aloud
papers.authors: Lihui Hu, Wenjie Chen, Travis Morgan Seale-Carlisle et al.
papers.summary: Reading words aloud makes them more memorable, and this study asked whether the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, a cognitive control region, is causally involved. In 40 adults, theta-burst TMS that reduces DLPFC excitability (cTBS) shrank the accuracy advantage for words read aloud compared with sham and excitatory stimulation, and modeling agreed. The authors call this the first causal evidence that DLPFC helps prioritize the distinctive information from speaking.
papers.abstract: Reading words aloud improves later recognition relative to reading them silently, a phenomenon known as the production effect. This advantage may reflect not only the distinctive sensorimotor information generated by production, but also cognitive control processes that prioritise this information during encoding. Given the central role of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) in supporting cognitive control, we tested whether this region causally contributes to the production effect using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). In a preregistered within-participant study, 40 adults completed three sessions in which TMS was delivered bilaterally to the DLPFC. They received continuous theta-burst stimulation (cTBS), expected to reduce DLPFC excitability; intermittent theta-burst stimulation (iTBS), expected to increase it; or sham stimulation. Participants then read words aloud or silently before completing an old/new recognition test with confidence and recollection judgements. There was a clear production effect: words read aloud were recognised more accurately and quickly, with greater confidence and more frequent recollection ratings, than words read silently. Crucially, cTBS reduced the accuracy advantage for aloud words relative to sham and iTBS. Exploratory receiver-operating-characteristic (ROC) and unequal-variance signal-detection (UVSD) modeling approaches provided converging evidence that cTBS reduced the memory advantage for words read aloud. Stimulation did not reliably affect responses to new words. These findings provide the first causal evidence that the DLPFC helps make words read aloud more memorable, consistent with a role for cognitive control in prioritising the distinctive information generated by speaking.

papers.title: Facilitation by Irrelevant Distractors Under High Perceptual Load: Suppression or Controlled Distractor Prioritization?
papers.authors: Greta Manini, Francisco Garre-Frutos, Fabiano Botta et al.
papers.summary: Under high perceptual load, irrelevant distractors sometimes speed up responses, which is usually read as distractor suppression, though the distractor sits outside the search array and suppression shouldn't help there. Reanalyzing open data from the Forster and Lavie task, the researchers found the speed-up was driven by distractors near the target, while far distractors led to more errors. That points to some kind of distractor prioritization instead, and challenges both the claim that high load blocks distractor processing and the usual reading of such speed-ups.
papers.abstract: Perceptual load theory is a key framework in visual attention research, demonstrating that under high-load conditions, fully irrelevant distractors are no longer processed and do not disrupt task performance. In our recent work (Manini et al., 2026), we replicated this effect. However, we also found that under high load, the distractor not only failed to impair performance but actually led to faster reaction times (RTs) in distractor-present trials. In the attentional capture literature, this reversed effect is typically considered to reflect distractor suppression. However, in the perceptual load task, where the distractor is placed outside the relevant search array, suppression should not logically lead to faster responses. Furthermore, the faster responses were accompanied by increased error rates, leading us to hypothesize that this reversed effect may reflect some form of distractor prioritization rather than distractor suppression. To test this hypothesis, we first analyzed the consistency of this effect across all available open-data resources using the Forster and Lavie (2008b) task. We then reanalyzed the same data, incorporating the spatial proximity between target and distractor as an additional variable: distractors appearing near the target strongly drove the reversed RT effect, while distractors presented far from the target led to increased error rates. These findings challenge the idea that high perceptual load prevents the processing of irrelevant stimuli. Moreover, they suggest that faster RTs in distractor-present conditions do not necessarily indicate distractor suppression, as commonly assumed in attentional capture research, offering new insight into the interpretation of behavioral observations in this field.

papers.title: Humans adaptively delay planning using cognitive maps
papers.authors: Paul B. Sharp, Eran Eldar
papers.summary: Planning is costly, so knowing when to hold off is useful. In a task where all actions were equally likely to reach the goal at certain moments, people in two preregistered studies learned to delay planning and got better with experience. A meta-control model suggests they don't learn this from outcomes, but by searching a cognitive map of the task to find where delaying is most valuable.
papers.abstract: Planning is an expensive computational operation that easily exhausts our cognitive resources. For this reason, it is critical to learn strategies to initiate planning wisely. To understand how humans adaptively initiate planning, we developed a task where humans can learn to delay planning at certain timepoints when all actions are equally likely to reach an instructed goal. Across two pre-registered studies, we show that humans adaptively delay planning, and improve in their ability to do so with experience. To explain this behavior, we formalize a model of the underlying meta-control computations. Our model demonstrates how strategies to delay planning are not learned from experienced outcomes, but rather, from searching a cognitive map of the task to determine at which points it is more valuable to delay control. We thus establish that humans can adaptively delay planning, and learn to do so by means of a cognitive map.

papers.title: Shared event representations in the Posterior Medial Network predict memory reinstatement, despite greater variability in older adults
papers.authors: Angelique I. Delarazan, Charan Ranganath, Zachariah Reagh
papers.summary: Younger and older adults watched a 26-minute TV episode and then freely recalled it in the scanner, letting the researchers compare neural patterns in the posterior medial network. Older adults recalled fewer specific details and were less similar to one another, though they resembled younger adults more than other older adults. In both age groups, people whose encoding patterns looked more like other viewers' showed stronger reinstatement during recall, linking shared representations at encoding to memory reinstatement despite more variability with age.
papers.abstract: Remembering an experience can reinstate patterns of neural activity from when the event originally occurred. During encoding, individuals show synchronized neural responses as events unfold, and greater synchrony across individuals has been linked to better memory. These shared neural responses may reflect aspects of an event that are consistently represented and could support later reinstatement. Yet whether greater similarity to others is associated with stronger reinstatement remains unclear, particularly in older adults, whose neural responses are more variable. Here, younger and older adults watched a 26-minute television episode and then freely recalled it while in the scanner. We measured moment-to-moment neural synchrony and event-specific spatial similarity across individuals in the posterior medial network (PMN). We then examined how these measures related to neural reinstatement and recall specificity. Older adults recalled fewer specific details and showed less similar event-specific encoding patterns to one another compared to younger adults. However, their patterns were more similar to those of younger adults than to those of other older adults. Both groups showed event-specific reinstatement. Importantly, individuals whose encoding patterns more closely resembled those of other viewers showed stronger reinstatement in both age groups. Greater neural synchrony was also associated with more specific recall in younger adults, although this relationship did not differ significantly between age groups. Together, these findings establish a link between how similarly experiences are represented across individuals during encoding and how strongly those representations are reinstated during remembering, even in the context of greater neural variability in older adulthood.

papers.title: Ranschburg Unrepeated
papers.authors: Robin Remouchamps, Steve Majerus, Benjamin Kowialiewski
papers.summary: The Ranschburg effect, where a repeated item in a memory list hurts recall, is often explained by response suppression. The researchers tried to extend it to visuospatial materials and to pin down its locus with forward and backward recall, but failed to replicate it, even with verbal materials and in situations where it had been seen before. Simulations suggest that if the effect exists, response suppression is unlikely to explain it, so its importance for working memory models is in question.
papers.abstract: In verbal working memory (WM), the second occurrence of an item in a memory list generally leads to impaired recall performance, a phenomenon called the “Ranschburg effect”. One explanation for this effect is response suppression, by which an item is removed from the set of retrieval candidates once recalled. The present study aimed at (1) determining the generality of this effect by extending it to the visuospatial domain, and (2) identifying the locus of the effect by using a forward/backward recall procedure. After a first unsuccessful attempt to replicate the Ranschburg effect using visuospatial stimuli, we sought to replicate the original effect using verbal materials. An additional series of three experiments failed to replicate the Ranschburg effect, including in experimental situations in which it had initially been observed. Simulations show that if the Ranschburg effect exists, it is unlikely to be explained by response suppression. The present study questions the importance of the Ranschburg effect for models of WM.

papers.title: Processing spoken prefixed words with obscured morphological identity and boundary: An auditory masked priming experiment
papers.authors: Dave Kenneth Tayao Cayado, Samantha Wray, Adam J. Chong et al.
papers.summary: In a Tagalog auditory masked priming experiment, the team tested whether spoken prefixed words are broken into morphemes even when sound changes blur the prefix and the boundary, like nasal assimilation or substitution. Priming was similar in size for unchanged, assimilated and substituted words, and wasn't found for monomorphemic words that merely overlap in sound, so the effect is morphological. This suggests decomposition in speech comprehension is robust to variable morphophonological changes.
papers.abstract: To comprehend speech, the auditory system segments a continuous input stream at various levels (e.g., sounds, words). Previous studies have shown that listeners also segment complex spoken words like treatment into their morphological units /ˈtriːt/+/mənt/, where there is a clear morphological boundary between /stem/+/affix/. Here, we report an auditory masked priming experiment in Tagalog investigating whether complex spoken words with obscured morphological identity and boundaries are segmented into morphemes. We compare the processing of prefixed words [1] without morphophonological alternations (NOCHANGE, e.g., /maŋ/+/híla/ becomes maŋhíla ‘to pull’), [2] with nasal ASSIMILATION obscuring prefix identity (e.g., /maŋ/+/búlag/ becomes mambúlag ‘to blind’), and [3] with nasal SUBSTITUTION obscuring both prefix and stem identities and their phonological boundary (e.g., /maŋ/+/túlak/ becomes manúlak ‘to push’). Crucially, these morphophonological alternations exhibit variability: nasal SUBSTITUTION is more likely for VOICELESS-initial stems than for VOICED-initial stems. We found significant priming effects of similar magnitude across NOCHANGE, ASSIMILATION, and SUBSTITUTION conditions. These effects are morphological in nature since no reliable priming was observed for monomorphemic word pairs with phonological overlap. Further, similar priming was found for both VOICELESS and VOICED SUBSTITUTION conditions. These findings unambiguously show that spoken complex words are decomposed into morphemes, thereby supporting auditory processing models and morphological theories which argue that morphologically complex words are stored and accessed as morphemes in the mental lexicon. Ultimately, we provide clear evidence that automatic decomposition in speech comprehension is robust in the face of variable morphophonological alternations that obscure prefix identity and morphological boundaries.

papers.title: A Hierarchical Dynamical Model of Learning, Forgetting, and Relearning
papers.authors: Howard Smith
papers.summary: This model tracks the probability of recalling individual items as they're learned, forgotten and relearned. Recall rises during study and falls exponentially during delays, with the forgetting rate itself changing through a hierarchy of processes on different timescales. It accounts for classic findings from Peterson and Peterson, Ebbinghaus and Perkins, spanning seconds to weeks, including serial position, list length and spacing effects, within one framework rather than as separate phenomena.
papers.abstract: The model developed here provides a quantitative account of a range of well-known findings on learning, forgetting, and relearning, spanning delays from seconds (e.g., Peterson &amp; Peterson, 1959) to weeks (e.g., Ebbinghaus, 1885/1964; Perkins, 1914). The model tracks the probability of recall of individual items as they are learned, forgotten, and relearned over time. During study, recall probability increases, whereas during retention intervals it declines exponentially. Crucially, the rate of this decline is not fixed but is governed by a forgetting exponent that itself changes across study and delay periods. These changes are organised within a hierarchy of interacting processes operating over multiple timescales, allowing recall dynamics to evolve systematically across study and delay. This structure allows the model to capture effects of serial position, list length, spacing, and long-term retention within a single framework. Although classic studies such as those of Ebbinghaus, Peterson and Peterson, and Perkins are often treated as demonstrations of separate phenomena, the present model shows that they can be understood as arising from a common set of underlying processes.

papers.title: Children Only 3 Years Can Succeed At Conditional "If, Then" Reasoning, Much Earlier Than Anyone Had Thought Possible
papers.authors: Daphne S. Ling, Cole D. Wong
papers.summary: Three-year-olds passed a conditional discrimination task (an "if this, then that" rule) when color was part of the object itself, which is 12-18 months earlier than past reports. They did better on that task when color and shape were integrated, but better on card sorting when the two were separated, even though the rule structure was the same in both. The pattern suggests that young children can reason conditionally but need perceptual support, and it argues against purely conceptual explanations for their earlier failures.
papers.abstract: We report results showing success at 3 years on conditional discrimination (CD) -- 12-18 months younger than previously reported. Three-year-olds succeeded when color was a property of the stimulus, rather than a property of the background, as in all past CD testing. Previously, we and others found children succeed on the dimensional change card sort (DCCS) test at 3 years -- 12-24 months earlier than previously reported -- by making color a property of the background, instead of a property of the stimulus, as in standard DCCS testing. Neither the change to CD or DCCS affected the rule structure or reasoning requirements of the task. This double dissociation, with 3-year-olds performing better on CD when color and shape were integrated but better on DCCS when color and shape were separated, indicates that when superficial stimulus properties are modified 3-year-olds can do conditional reasoning and grasp a hierarchical rule structure - but they seem to need perceptual boot-strapping to do that. Children of 3 years evidently have difficulty mentally separating physical dimensions (e.g., color and shape) of the same object and difficulty mentally integrating physical dimensions not part of the same object. These results provide the strongest evidence to date against conceptual accounts of why children of 3 years fail conditional discrimination or card sorting.

papers.title: The influence of attention on visual statistical learning and vice versa: Insights from frequency-based grouping as revealed by EEG frequency tagging
papers.authors: Elena Greatti, Davide Crepaldi
papers.summary: Using EEG frequency tagging, which tracks brain activity that synchronizes with a stream's structure, the researchers asked how statistical learning and attention interact. Brain entrainment appeared only for structured streams, and improvement on a concurrent 3-back task was slower when structure was present, so picking up regularities seems to cost a little attention. Going the other way, making the task harder had no detectable effect on neural tracking, so the relationship looks asymmetric.
papers.abstract: The human brain readily captures regularities in the environment. It is not clear, however, whether and how this skill—statistical learning—interacts with attention. We addressed this issue by leveraging neural entrainment, the synchronization of brain activity with statistical structure. In Study 1, we asked whether sensitivity to a frequency-based regularity, created by embedding low-frequency items among higher-frequency items, competes for attentional resources with a concurrent task. Participants viewed structured or random visual streams while performing a 3-back color matching task. Neural entrainment emerged only for structured streams, demonstrating sensitivity to the frequency structure. Improvement in the concurrent task, indexed by decreasing response times, unfolded more slowly when structure was present, suggesting that detecting statistical regularities drew attention away from the 3-back color matching task. In Study 2, we tested the reverse connection—whether taxing attention with a more difficult task impairs the neural tracking of statistical structure. We compared entrainment during an easier color-change detection task and a more difficult 3-back color matching task. We observed no detectable effect of attentional load on neural entrainment. These findings reveal an asymmetric relationship between attention and frequency-based statistical learning: detecting structure imposes a modest attentional cost on a concurrent behavioral task, whereas the online neural tracking of regularities appears to be unaffected by increased attentional demands.

papers.title: Tuning flexibility of target templates, not of distractor templates
papers.authors: Sizhu Han, Lea Marie Schmitt, Anna Schubö
papers.summary: In two experiments with color cues of varying precision, the researchers tested how flexibly people adjust their search templates for targets versus distractors. Positive cues helped steadily at small cue-target differences, but at larger differences the best selection shifted toward colors displaced away from the distractor. Negative cues gave little benefit and weren't systematically affected by precision or direction, which suggests target templates are much more adaptable than distractor templates.
papers.abstract: Attentional templates guide visual search by biasing attention toward target features and away from distractors, yet how these templates adjust as a function of cue precision and directional deviation remains poorly understood. In two experiments, we manipulated cue precision to assess how imprecise color-based templates guide voluntary attentional selection. With positive cues (indicating the target template), robust benefits were stable at small cue–target deviations (≤36°), but shifted to an optimal tuning pattern at larger deviations (≥48°), where selection favored cues displaced away from distractor features. In contrast, negative cues (indicating the distractor template) yielded little benefit and no systematic modulation by cue precision or direction. These results indicate that target templates flexibly shift from coarse, category-like representations to optimally tuned configurations when target-distractor discriminability is challenged. Together, these findings reveal distinct mechanisms and varying degrees of flexibility underlying target versus distractor templates in voluntary visual search.

papers.title: Cue-guided attention modulates neural responses to distracting features
papers.authors: Sizhu Han, Anna Schubö
papers.summary: Can people suppress a distractor feature in advance when told what it will be? Behaviorally, negative cues helped in a hard search with 8 relevant items but not an easy one with 4, and EEG showed an early suppression signal (distractor PD) in people who benefited, while those who were slowed showed a capture-like signal (N2pc) on slow trials. Stronger alpha lateralization went with bigger individual benefits, so using negative cues seems to be a strategic choice that depends on task demands and individual control ability.
papers.abstract: The impact of prior knowledge about an upcoming distractor (i.e., a negative cue) on performance in a subsequent search task has yielded mixed results. A central question is whether negatively cued features can be preemptively suppressed (i.e., before distractors capture attention) or whether they initially capture attention followed by reactive distractor handling (i.e., after distractors capture attention). Notably, negative cueing benefits tend to emerge when the search task is difficult, yet most prior electrophysiological studies have employed easy search tasks that may discourage negative cue use. Therefore, direct neural evidence for negative cueing effects under difficult search is rare. To address this gap, we conducted two experiments. Experiment 1 manipulated task difficulty by varying the number of task-relevant items while keeping the overall set size constant. Results revealed that negative cues enhanced search efficiency in difficult search (8 task-relevant items), but not in easy search (4 items), suggesting that negative cueing benefits depended on the number of items requiring attention rather than overall set size. Experiment 2 employed EEG during difficult search to delineate the neural underpinnings of distractor processing. ERP results showed that negatively cued distractors elicited a reliable early distractor PD in participants showing a cueing benefit in RT but a distractor N2pc on slow-response trials in participants showing RT cost. While preparatory alpha activity did not differ by cue type, stronger alpha lateralization was associated with larger cueing benefits at the individual level. Collectively, these findings suggest that negative cue use is a flexible, strategic and active process, with its deployment contingent on both task demands and individual differences in control capacity.

papers.title: Traveling back and forth through time: oscillatory brain patterns distinguish directional cued recall
papers.authors: Jeffrey D Johnson
papers.summary: Participants learned word lists and then used a cue word to recall either the next word (forward) or the previous one (backward), with performance matched across directions. Using EEG and pattern classification, the researchers could tell forward from backward retrieval from high-frequency gamma-band activity just before the response. This suggests that moving through memory in different temporal directions engages distinguishable neural processes, with implications for how time is represented in episodic memory.
papers.abstract: It is well established that episodic memory involves forming associations among stimuli within an event and between the event and its spatial and temporal context and that those associations can subsequently guide the strategies and search processes that lead to successful retrieval. While countless studies have characterized the neurocognitive correlates of relational memory, how retrieval precisely relies on the associations formed between consecutive events, as well as their correspondence with a representation of past time, is less understood. The current study sought to test how transitions are made across memories according to time by directly contrasting, behaviorally and neurally, retrieval in the forward versus backward directions. A list-learning paradigm was employed with immediate cued recall tasks in which subjects had to use cue words to recall those that came next (forward) or previously (backward) in the list. Scalp EEG data acquired just before the recalled words had to be reported was then used, in combination with multivariate pattern-classification analysis (MVPA), to distinguish neural activity related to retrieval deliberation and search processes. The main results provide novel evidence that, even while equating behavioral performance across retrieval direction, high-frequency (gamma-band) oscillatory EEG activity distinguishes forward and backward retrieval. Implications of the findings are discussed in relation to other, widely-used experimental and neuropsychological tasks (e.g., serial and free recall), as well as to work on understanding the broader role of time (i.e., past versus future) in episodic memory.

papers.title: Learning What Matters: Goal certainty shapes working memory prioritization
papers.authors: Cathy Zhang, Ata Baris Karagoz, Wouter Kool
papers.summary: In a task where a hidden rule about stimulus features changed without warning, participants (N = 104) judged stimuli and occasionally reproduced the color, shape, and motion of the previous one. As a reinforcement-learning model's estimate of rule certainty rose, memory for the irrelevant features declined. Modeling showed this came from relevant features being more likely to be kept and irrelevant ones less likely, with little change in precision. So learning what matters changes what gets retained rather than how sharply it is stored.
papers.abstract: Cognitive resources are limited, yet people face an abundance of information. Often, which information matters is not stated and can change over time, so people must learn it through experience. This creates a tradeoff: uncertainty requires broad maintenance of multiple information sources, whereas certainty allows resources to be allocated more selectively. Does this reorganization of resources reflect enhancement of relevant information, degradation of irrelevant information, or both? Working memory provides a window into this process because differences in attentional priority should be reflected in what is remembered. To address these questions, we developed the Continuously Assessed Rule Inference Task, in which participants (N = 104) judged whether multidimensional stimuli followed a hidden rule that changed without warning, requiring them to continually update their beliefs about which information was relevant. On intermittent probe trials, participants reproduced the color, shape, and motion direction of the preceding stimulus. A reinforcement-learning model estimated trial-by-trial rule certainty from participants’ choices. As certainty increased, rule judgments relied more on evidence from the rule-defining (active) dimension, and memory for inactive features declined. A mixture model showed that active features became more likely to be retained, and inactive features less likely, with little evidence that the precision of retained features changed. These findings suggest that learning what matters reorganizes working memory by changing which information is retained, rather than how precisely it is represented. This shift from broad to selective maintenance may reflect a tradeoff between flexibility under uncertainty and efficiency once relevant information has been identified.

papers.title: An MDS-REM Model for Predicting Individual-Item Perceptual Old-New Recognition
papers.authors: Robert Nosofsky, Adam F Osth
papers.summary: The REM recognition memory model usually predicts results for whole classes of items through simulation. This work proposes an MDS-REM version in which each item is a point in a multidimensional similarity space, plus item-specific distinctive features, using continuous probability densities instead of a geometric distribution. Tested on three earlier perceptual recognition datasets, it predicted performance reasonably well for individual items or categories, including how similarity relations and distinctive features affect both hits and false alarms.
papers.abstract: The Retrieving Effectively for Memory (REM) model (Shiffrin &amp; Stevyers, 1997) is an extremely influential model of old-new recognition memory based on Bayesian reasoning principles that provides a comprehensive account of diverse memory phenomena. However, a limitation of extant versions of the model is that it does not provide accounts of recognition memory at the level of individual items based on their precise positions in multidimensional similarity space and their possession of item-specific distinctive features. Instead, it assumes a geometric probability distribution for generating hypothetical features and relies on computer simulation to generate predictions of patterns of results for large classes of items and experimental manipulations. Here we move in the direction of filling that gap by proposing a REM-like model in which individual items are represented in one-to-one correspondence as points in multidimensional similarity (MDS) spaces and in which information regarding distinctive features possessed by individual objects is also provided. Rather than using the geometric-probability distribution envisioned by Shiffrin and Steyvers, this “MDS-REM” model uses continuous probability density functions defined over the continuous-dimension MDS spaces. The model is tested using data sets from three previously reported perceptual old-new recognition studies and provides reasonably accurate predictions of performance at the level of individual items or categories, including accounts of how both false-alarm and hit rates are influenced by detailed similarity relations among items and their possession of item-specific distinctive features.

papers.title: Pattern Completion of Occluded Objects Transforms Retrieval into Learning
papers.authors: Jennifer Gove, David E. Huber, Rosemary Cowell
papers.summary: People studied whole objects and then either restudied them or practiced retrieving them from a "peephole" view that showed only part of the object. The peephole-practiced objects were remembered better later, a visual testing effect that appeared without help from conceptual information. The effect vanished when retrieval didn't require completing the pattern from a partial view, suggesting that the visual pattern completion we use to recognize occluded objects also drives learning.
papers.abstract: Recognizing a partially occluded object is effortless and automatic: visual cortex fills in the missing parts to infer a recognizable whole. We tested whether part-to-whole visual pattern completion constitutes not just a retrieval operation, but also a learning mechanism. Participants studied whole objects, after which each object was assigned either to retrieval practice, cued by a circular aperture offering a “peephole” view, or to restudy. At final test, retrieval-practiced (peephole-cued) objects were better remembered than restudied objects – a visual testing effect. The task eliminated the utility of conceptual information, suggesting that this testing effect occurs without semantic mediation, contrary to prominent theories. Critically, when retrieval no longer required pattern completion—retrieval without a peephole cue—the testing effect disappeared. Thus, we report a non-semantically mediated visual testing effect driven by occlusion-induced pattern completion. We suggest that visual pattern completion supports not only occluded object recognition, but also robust visual learning.

papers.title: Diverse Mechanisms of Adaptive Variability in Human Behavior
papers.authors: Janne Reynders, Tom Verguts, Senne Braem
papers.summary: The researchers built a hide-and-seek task to compare five possible ways people produce variable behavior: random choice, fast reinforcement learning, and memory for action frequencies, sequence frequencies, or specific episodes. Across three experiments (N = 290), people raised their learning rate in volatile environments but relied more on stochasticity, action-frequency memory, and episodic memory in adversarial ones. Adaptive variability therefore doesn't seem to be one mechanism but a flexible mix that depends on the environment's demands.
papers.abstract: Adaptive variability in behavior is crucial when environments promote unpredictability, yet its underlying cognitive mechanisms remain poorly understood. Volatile and adversarial environments can elicit variability by abrupt rule switches and explicitly reinforcing variable choices, respectively; however, literature lacks paradigms, computational models, and data to investigate and compare how (human) agents address such challenges. We introduce a novel hide-and-seek paradigm and use computational modeling to disentangle five candidate cognitive mechanisms of variability: stochastic choice, fast reinforcement learning, action-frequency-based memory, sequence-frequency-based memory, and episodic memory. Across three experiments (N = 290), we show that participants flexibly increased learning rate in volatile environments, but stochasticity, action-frequency-based memory, and reliance on episodic memory in adversarial environments. For the first time, these findings uncover that adaptive variability is not a unitary phenomenon but instead emerges from the flexible recruitment of multiple cognitive mechanisms as environmental demands intensify.

papers.title: Proactive Control and the Processing of English Wh-Dependencies: A Web-Based Behavioral Study
papers.authors: Keng-Yu Lin, Edith Kaan
papers.summary: Participants did either a more or less proactive version of the AX-CPT (a cognitive control task) and then read English wh-question sentences, some with filled gaps that disrupt parsing. The control manipulation clearly worked in the AX-CPT, but it didn't change later sentence reading. Unlike in earlier studies, a filled-gap effect did show up at the subject position, which hints that participants were more proactive overall, perhaps because of the control task.
papers.abstract: Previous studies have found that the engagement of domain-general cognitive control facilitates the solution of sentence ambiguities. This web-based behavioral study investigated the interplay between general cognitive control and linguistic processing. We examined the interactions between proactive control and processing of English wh-dependencies. We reasoned that if processing English wh-dependencies engages proactive control, we should observe differences in reaction times and/or accuracy during processing when proactive control is exercised to different extents.To this end, we manipulated participants’ proactive control mode by asking them to perform one of the two variants (less vs. more proactive versions) of the AX-Continuous Performance Task (AX-CPT), right after which they read English wh-dependency sentences in a self-paced manner. We also manipulated the gap type (filled vs. control) of the English wh-dependency sentences: filled gaps induce parsing disruptions while control gaps do not. Our AX-CPT results revealed that participants were in distinct proactive control modes under our manipulation; however, such differences did not modulate the subsequent sentence reading task. We did observe a filled gap effect at the subject position, in contrast to previous studies. This suggests that our participants were more proactive than those in prior studies, possibly due to the proactivity manipulation task.

papers.title: Memorability as an Emergent Property: How Representational Structure Creates Apparent Intrinsic Effects
papers.authors: Dyllan Simpson, John Wixted, Timothy F. Brady
papers.summary: Memorability, the tendency for some images or words to be remembered reliably better than others, is usually treated as an intrinsic property of the items. Simulations with a global matching memory model, and behavioral experiments, show it can arise from distinctiveness within a given stimulus set: changing the set's similarity structure could even flip memorability rankings. Features thought to be intrinsically memorable turned out to be the most distinctive in standard databases, and a new image set with more even distinctiveness weakened those relationships.
papers.abstract: Some pictures, videos, faces, voices, and words are reliably remembered better than others, a phenomenon known as memorability. This has been widely interpreted as reflecting a stable, intrinsic property of the stimuli themselves. Here we argue that this consistency is better explained by the relational structure of the stimulus sets used to measure memorability, rather than as an intrinsic property of the items. Using simulations with a global matching model of recognition memory, we show that apparent intrinsic memorability emerges naturally from distinctiveness — how dissimilar an item is from others in a given set of encoded images — without any stimulus-intrinsic mechanism. In behavioral experiments, we demonstrate that manipulating the similarity structure of image sets can invert memorability rankings, making previously memorable images forgettable and vice versa. We also show that features previously identified as intrinsically memorable (such as “body-part related”) are the most representationally distinctive features in standard databases, explaining their memorability. To address these large variations in distinctiveness we created a new image set that reduced variability in representational distinctiveness, and found it significantly diminishes all feature-memorability relationships. These findings suggest that memorability is not a fixed attribute of items themselves, but an emergent property of which items are distinctive within the context, with implications for how we attribute stable psychological properties to stimuli more broadly.

papers.title: Meaningfulness shapes strategic memory use
papers.authors: Luzi Xu, Surya Gayet, Andre Sahakian et al.
papers.summary: When people can look back at a display as they copy it, they usually hold only 1-2 items in memory at a time. In two experiments with a copying task, meaningful real-world objects raised memory use to about 3.8 items per look, compared with about 2.5 for meaningless objects matched on low-level visual features. So the advantage of meaningful objects goes beyond raw capacity and changes how people trade off remembering against re-checking.
papers.abstract: Recent studies show that working memory for meaningful real-world objects can far exceed traditional capacity limits (~4 items) under experimental conditions where items are briefly presented. In everyday life, however, information often remains accessible, and observers freely choose how much to remember now and how much to inspect later. Under such unconstrained conditions, people typically memorize only 1–2 items at a time, far below maximum capacity. Here, we asked how meaningfulness influences strategic memory use during unconstrained memory-guided behavior. Using a copying task that allows for reinspections of the display, we compared meaningful real‑world objects with meaningless (novel‑but‑realistic) objects matched on low‑level visual features. Across two experiments, meaningfulness increased memory use, boosting it from ~2.5 items (meaningless objects) to ~3.8 items (meaningful objects) per sampling. Thus, the advantage of real‑world objects extends beyond capacity: it changes how people balance memory use against re-sampling of information in natural behavior.

papers.title: Early visual cortex is not functionally necessary for temporal attention: A TMS study
papers.authors: Lee, H.-H., Carrasco, M.
papers.summary: To test whether early visual cortex (V1/V2) is causally needed for temporal attention, the researchers applied double-pulse TMS at the time of the first stimulus, the second, both, or neither while people did an orientation task with temporal precues. The benefits of temporal attention stayed robust in every TMS condition, and pupil dilation patterns confirmed that the stimulation did something physiologically. This is causal evidence that early visual cortex isn't functionally necessary for endogenous temporal attention.
papers.abstract: Temporal attention enhances the selective processing of information at a specific point in time and improves perception. Previous neuroimaging studies investigating its neural mechanisms have either conflated temporal attention with temporal expectation or provided correlational evidence. Thus, whether early visual cortex is functionally necessary for temporal attention remains unknown. Here, we combined psychophysics with transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) to examine whether V1/V2 are functionally necessary and play a causal role in temporal attention. Observers performed an orientation-discrimination task in which two consecutive stimuli, T1 and T2, were presented in the periphery, preceded by a precue providing either valid or neutral temporal information. Double-pulse TMS was delivered under four conditions: at T1 (T1-TMS), at T2 (T2-TMS), at both T1 and T2 (both-TMS), or not at all (none-TMS), to assess its effects on temporal attention and the efficacy of the stimulation was verified by pupil size analysis. Behavioral results revealed robust temporal attention benefits on d', reaction time, and the Balanced Integration Score (BIS) across all four TMS conditions, indicating that the benefits of temporal attention were unaffected by occipital TMS. Furthermore, pupil dilation was largest in the both-TMS condition, followed by the T1-TMS and T2-TMS conditions, and smallest in the none-TMS condition, providing physiological verification of the stimulation protocol. Together, these findings reveal the first causal evidence that the early visual cortex is not functionally necessary for endogenous temporal attention.

papers.title: Metarepresentation and the puzzle of desire-attribution
papers.authors: Evan Westra, Gavin Robert Foster
papers.summary: Children seem to attribute desires earlier than beliefs, which is puzzling because the standard philosophical view gives both the same metarepresentational structure. The paper reviews three possible solutions and their limitations, then proposes a non-metarepresentational account in which young children's desire concept rests on a kind of representation called modal affordances.
papers.abstract: Among theory-of-mind researchers, it's widely agreed that children acquire the capacity to attribute desires well before they acquire the capacity to attribute beliefs. This suggests that there is something about the concept of desire that makes it less cognitively challenging than the concept of belief, but what could that be? One possibility is that the difference has something to do with the development of the capacity for metarepresentation, but this just raises more questions: according to the standard philosophical model of the propositional attitudes, the concepts of belief and desire share the same basic metarepresentational structure. First, we review three potential solutions to this developmental puzzle and discuss their limitations. Then we propose a novel non-metarepresentational account of young children's concept of desire that grounds the contents of desire attributions in a type of representation that we call modal affordances.

papers.title: Heterogeneity in holistic face processing disruptions in developmental prosopagnosia
papers.authors: Angus F. Chapman, Lauren C. Bell, Bradley Duchaine et al.
papers.summary: In a large sample of people with developmental prosopagnosia (N = 113), the researchers measured three signature effects of holistic face processing: inversion, composite, and part-whole. All three were reduced at the group level, though the composite effect was slightly less robust, and there was little evidence the reductions tracked severity. Few individuals fell in the impaired range, so weaker holistic processing is common in DP but doesn't appear to be necessary for it.
papers.abstract: Developmental prosopagnosia (DP) is a striking disorder characterised by lifelong deficits in face recognition. Research into the nature of DP has broad implications for understanding interrelated theoretical issues in vision, neural organisation, and development. One long-standing but unresolved question is whether holistic face processing, the integration of individual face features into a unified whole, is compromised in DP. Here, we test a large sample of DPs (N = 113), using the three signature effects of holistic processing: the inversion, composite, and part-whole effects. This approach allows us to characterise the extent and pattern of holistic reductions across multiple effects within the same sample and to assess relationships between them. We found that holistic processing is reduced across all three effects in DP. The magnitude of reductions varied across the different effects; however, follow-up analyses indicated that reductions in the composite effect were slightly less robust. We found little evidence linking these reductions to DP severity, though limited reliability in the holistic measures may constrain these conclusions. While we observed reductions in holistic processing at the group level, few individual DPs met the thresholds for impairment. Our findings suggest that DP is associated with weaker holistic effects, but do not support the notion that impairments in holistic processing are necessary for DP.

papers.title: Communication about color over the life span
papers.authors: Angela M. Brown, Delwin T. Lindsey
papers.summary: Participants aged 3 to 72 played a color communication game: they named color samples, then picked colors from a palette based on either their own earlier names or someone else's. Vocabulary size, self-communication accuracy and interpersonal accuracy all kept growing until at least age 21 and tracked each other closely. A model predicted that interpersonal performance wouldn't change with age, but it did improve, which suggests that understanding other people's color terms is a separate ability from producing your own, and the two mature independently.
papers.abstract: Color communication is more than a naming game where the informant names each color: the color terms must also be understood by the listener. Here, we studied how participants' productive and receptive vocabularies affect communication about color over the life span. Human participants, 3-72 years old, played a color communication game. As "senders", participants named 15 or 30 color samples presented singly. Then, as "receivers", they selected from their palette of 15 or 30 colors the sample that corresponded to color term "messages," which were either their own color terms (self-communication) or another participant's color terms (interpersonal communication). The number of color terms in participants' vocabularies, their fraction correct performance for self-communication, and their fraction correct for interpersonal communication, all matured continuously until at least age 21, and were highly correlated with each other. Simulations using a quantitative model of the communication task showed that performance for self-communication was determined by the number of color terms the participant provided in the color-naming phase (color term production), with some forgetting of how they had previously named the samples. The simulation predicted no association between participant age and performance on the interpersonal communication task. Contrary to that prediction, interpersonal communication improved throughout the age range. Further analysis showed that performance for interpersonal communication was independently controlled by life-long improvement in participants' ability to understand terms provided by others (color term comprehension). Therefore, color term production and color term comprehension are distinct abilities, which mature independently across the life span.

papers.title: How explanations evolve: Social learning and the explore–exploit trade-off
papers.authors: Kara Kedrick, Kevin J.S. Zollman, Simon DeDeo
papers.summary: When people explain something odd, they often already have others' explanations in hand, and this work asks how those explanations steer what they do next. In a two-stage transmission experiment (101 people wrote explanations, then 995 others read pairs of them before writing their own), people tended to imitate when at least one explanation was strong, especially when it sat next to a weak one. They blended ideas when both were good and distinct, and struck out on their own when both were weak and distinct. It's a neat account of how a group's shared explanations can help or stall collective exploration.
papers.abstract: Explanations are social objects, and when people try to explain something, they usually have at hand the explanations that others have tried before. We present a theory of how people use the explanations they encounter as clues to the broader landscape of possible explanations for the phenomenon to hand, which in turn informs their decisions about how and when to forage further for the explanations they wish to adopt. The challenge of coming up with novel explanations draws people to exploit or imitate appealing ones they have already encountered; this draw increases as less appealing alternatives become more distant (the "strawman" effect). Conversely, when presented with distinct, high-quality explanations, people can synthesize them, recombining the appealing features in new ways. We test and confirm these predictions using a two-stage transmission chain experiment. In Stage One, 101 participants were asked to explain unusual scenarios. In Stage Two, a separate group of 995 participants were asked to explain the same scenarios after reading pairs of explanations drawn from Stage One. We found that participants in Stage Two were more likely to exploit, or imitate, explanations when at least one was high in quality and particularly when it was paired with a weaker alternative. Participants were also more likely to synthesize perspectives from prior explanations when the two explanations were both high-quality and conceptually distinct. In contrast, participants were more likely to explore, or diverge, from prior explanations when the two explanations were both of low quality and distinct. Our work provides new insight into how collective exploration can be promoted, or stalled, by implicit information about what is yet to be discovered.

papers.title: Sleep promotes sublexical learning and clears out by-products of word recognition
papers.authors: Arthur G. Samuel, Nicolas Dumay
papers.summary: Across six experiments, the researchers looked at how recently heard speech changes sensitivity to similar sounds and words, and whether sleep matters. Sound-level (sublexical) sensitivity only helped processing of related pseudowords after sleep, while active word representations hurt processing of near-neighbor pseudowords right away and after 12 hours awake, but not after 12 hours that included sleep. So sleep seems to strengthen the new sound-level learning while clearing out lingering word-level activation.
papers.abstract: Most models of spoken word recognition include both lexical and sublexical representations. When speech input is consistent with a given lexical or sublexical representation, that representation's activation increases, with recognition dependent on reaching some absolute or relative activation level. After a representation has been activated during perception, it remains sensitive to similar subsequent input for some period of time. In the current study we report six experiments that investigate the time course of this increased sensitivity, with sleep as a potential moderating factor. Elevated sensitivity of sublexical representations facilitates processing of other pseudowords that contain these sounds, but a period of sleep is needed for this effect to emerge. In contrast, active lexical representations impair processing of pseudowords that only differ by one segment. Such impairment is observed immediately and after delays of 12 h without sleep, but not if the 12 h include sleep; sleep appears to clear out already-established representations. Our findings demonstrate that sublexical and lexical representations, once engaged during speech perception, become more sensitive to subsequent similar input, with the durability of the sensitivity differing as a function of lexical status and wake/sleep after the initial perceptual exposure. Sleep supports the new, and clears out the old.

papers.title: Enduring Hard Times: Task Difficulty Promotes Active Maintenance of Response-Response Bindings
papers.authors: Christoph Felix Geissler, Lars-Michael Schöpper, Birte Moeller et al.

papers.title: Equating interference on an initial test eliminates the negation-induced forgetting effect.
papers.authors: Rachel E. Dianiska, Christian A. Meissner, Jason C. K. Chan
papers.summary: Negation-induced forgetting is the finding that an object tied to a correctly negated feature ("the ashtray was not empty") is more likely to be misremembered as unstudied than one tied to an affirmed feature. Across six experiments, the effect appeared whenever the standard procedure was used, but vanished once the initial test statements were rewritten so affirmed and negated versions both mentioned a congruent and an incongruent feature. That points to interference from the extra incongruent feature, rather than inhibition, as the source of the forgetting.
papers.abstract: Items that are associated with a correct feature negation on an intervening test are more likely to be misremembered as having not been studied than items that are associated with a correct feature affirmation. An inhibition-based mechanism has been suggested to underlie this "negation-induced forgetting" effect. In a series of six experiments, we extend this line of work and examine whether negation-induced forgetting is replicable in both the original paradigm and a new paradigm. We also test the potential for an alternative, interference-based account of negation-induced forgetting. In the new paradigm, participants studied images of simple objects and then completed an initial yes-no test about features of the studied objects (e.g., "the ashtray was empty"). In some experiments, feature statements were manipulated to include only a congruent/affirmed or incongruent/negated feature (standard phrasing) or were rephrased to include both congruent and incongruent features within the same statement (interference-equated phrasing). After a brief delay, participants indicated whether each object (e.g., "ashtray") had been studied or not. Negation-induced forgetting was observed in all experiments when the standard procedure was used; however, this effect was eliminated when we adapted the initial test to account for the presence of an interfering feature in negated statements. These experiments suggest that the memory impairment following a correct negation is due to interference from an incongruent feature that is present in negated statements but not in affirmed statements.
