papers.title: Expectation is jointly shaped by global and transitional probabilities
papers.authors: Austin Luor, Frederic Dick, Lori L. Holt
papers.summary: Listeners heard a cue tone and then a short or long target tone, and judged the target's duration while tone pitch carried hidden statistical patterns irrelevant to the task. Decisions were faster when the cue's pitch predicted the target's pitch through a high transitional probability, and also when the target pitch was common overall. The two effects were similar in size but didn't simply add up, showing that people pick up several layers of regularity even along a dimension they aren't asked to attend to.
papers.abstract: Humans implicitly extract statistical regularities from sensory input across multiple perceptual dimensions. But it is unclear how statistical learning builds expectations that in turn may affect perceptual decisions, especially in the context of co-occurring regularities. In audition both transitional probabilities (across successive sounds) and global probabilities (sounds’ overall frequency of occurrence) shape perception. Here, we investigated how these two forms of statistical structure jointly influence perceptual judgments. Participants heard a 70-ms cue tone followed by a 50-ms or 90-ms target tone and judged whether the target tone was short or long. Statistical regularities were embedded along a task-irrelevant dimension, tone frequency, allowing for assessment of how implicit statistical learning unfolds when regularities are orthogonal to task goals. A sensory match in cue and target tone frequencies provided no advantage to duration decision response times. However, duration decisions were faster when cue tone frequency predicted target tone frequency across a high transitional probability. Target tones with high global probability drove faster duration decisions compared to those with low global probability. The combined evidence indicates that global target probability and cue–target transitional probability exerted similar magnitude effects, but their combined influence was not additive. Thus, even in active tasks demanding attention to a specific dimension (duration), listeners implicitly learn statistical structure along an irrelevant dimension (frequency) and track multiple regularities. This work advances our understanding of how layered statistical regularities guide prediction in goal-directed listening contexts.

papers.title: Supervisory control of declarative and procedural responding
papers.authors: F. Gregory Ashby
papers.summary: If the brain has separate learning systems, such as an explicit rule-based one and a procedural one, something has to decide which is in charge. The researchers tested several models of that switching against empirical benchmarks in categorization. Only models with a switch cost, which changed systems when the rule system's accuracy fell below a criterion while the procedural system was doing reasonably well, passed every test. They suggest this as a new class of switching models that could be added to existing multiple-systems frameworks such as COVIS or ATRIUM.
papers.abstract: There is overwhelming evidence that multiple systems mediate human learning. If so, then a problem of fundamental importance is to determine how control is passed back and forth among these systems. Although more research is needed, existing evidence suggests that system switching does occur, but is much less common than existing models assume, and that the bias toward strategies mediated by declarative memory is stronger than previously assumed. These shortcomings are addressed by testing a variety of different alternative models of system switching against several empirical benchmarks. The models all assumed separate explicit-rule and procedural/exemplar-similarity categorization systems. The only models that passed all benchmark tests incorporated a switch cost and switched systems when explicit-system accuracy dropped below a criterion value and procedural system accuracy was simultaneously reasonably high. This research suggests a new class of system-switching models, which could be incorporated into any existing multiple-systems model (e.g., COVIS or ATRIUM), and that is much more consistent with existing data than current models.

papers.title: Revealing the hidden spatial distribution of visual attention through pupillometry
papers.authors: Marleen Abbestee, Christoph Strauch, Chris L. E. Paffen et al.
papers.summary: Pupil size shifts depending on whether you attend to a bright or dark location, and this work uses that to track the spread of attention over time. With a luminance-tagged background, pupil responses followed expansions and contractions of attentional breadth in one experiment, and in another seemed able to tell a ring-shaped focus from a circular one. The upshot is a continuous, objective way to measure the attentional field that can be paired with other tasks.
papers.abstract: Visual attention selects which visual information is processed at a given moment. Its spatial distribution, the size and shape, constitute the attentional field. This field can be flexibly adjusted and is central to everyday behavior, yet how it changes over time is challenging to capture. In the present study, we introduce a pupillometry approach that uses luminance tagging to track changes in the attentional field continuously. Previous work has shown that attending to a brighter location causes pupil constriction compared to attending a darker location. Here, we extend these findings by demonstrating that this technique can capture changes in the attentional field. In Experiment 1, a static luminance-tagged background was used to track expansions and contractions of attentional breadth indirectly. In Experiment 2, this method appeared sensitive to changes in attentional shape, suggesting it could distinguish an annular from a circular attentional distribution. Together, this shows that luminance tagging combined with pupillometry provides a continuous and objective measure of attentional field allocations that can be flexibly combined with secondary tasks.

papers.title: Do you know what you’re looking for? Guiding templates are imprecise for both simple and real-world stimuli
papers.authors: Jessica N. Goetz, Mark B. Neider
papers.summary: Across three preregistered experiments, the researchers tested whether the mental template guiding visual search is a precise copy of the target, using both colored circles and real-world objects. In every case the template was coarser than the target, guiding attention to a broader range of features, and it got coarser still when the initially encoded target was less precise. Fuzzy templates therefore seem to be a general feature of efficient search, not a quirk of simple stimuli.
papers.abstract: Recent research has found evidence that a highly veridical representation of the target is not used to guide attention. Rather, the template is broadly tuned to guide attention to a wider range of feature values than characterized by the target. In three experiments, we investigated whether a veridical representation of target features is used to guide attention when the target is a real-world object. In Experiment 1, we examined the imprecision of the guiding template when searching for real-world objects. We compared the coarseness of the guiding template across colored circles and real-world objects in Experiment 2. In Experiment 3, we evaluated if the accuracy of the encoded target item affected the coarseness of the guiding template. We found evidence across all three experiments that the guiding template does not represent the target veridically and that the coarseness of the template is affected by the initial precision of the target representation. The results support prior research suggesting that a coarser template may be inherent to efficient guidance regardless of stimulus type. Open Practices Statement The data for all three experiments are available in the Open Science Framework (OSF) repository ( https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/PBG4U ). All three experiments were preregistered and can be found in the same repository.

papers.title: Are cueing effects really “negligible” when accuracy is emphasized and single masks eliminate uncertainty about target location?
papers.authors: Şimal Dölek, Seema Prasad, John Christie et al.
papers.summary: An older study found negligible benefits of spatial pre-cues when a single mask removed location uncertainty, which was taken as support for the idea that cues just reduce uncertainty. A more recent one found clear cueing effects under similar conditions. Here, two preregistered experiments that stressed either speed or accuracy found robust cueing effects in both reaction time and accuracy with single masks. This supports signal enhancement as one mechanism behind cueing, though the authors allow that more than one mechanism may be at work.
papers.abstract: Does spatial attention operate primarily by minimizing decision-related noise or by enhancing information from the attended location? While emphasizing and only reporting accuracy, Shiu and Pashler (Journal of Experimental Psychology. Human Perception and Performance, 20 (5), 1037-1054, 1994) found "negligible" effects of spatial pre-cues when uncertainty about the target's location was eliminated by a single mask, a finding often cited in favor of the idea that spatial pre-cues improve performance by reducing uncertainty (and not by signal enhancement). In a similar, single-mask condition, and while emphasizing reaction time (RT), Prasad and Hommel (Experimental Psychology, 71 (3):135-143, 2024), found significant cueing effects in reaction time and accuracy, which is consistent with signal enhancement. Stimulated by this empirical discrepancy, we implemented the fundamental methods of these studies to explore how invalid versus valid cues affected participant RT and accuracy. In each of two experiments we included a speed-stress manipulation: emphasizing response speed in one group and accuracy in the other. In Experiment 1, clear cueing effects were found in RT and accuracy across all conditions. In Experiment 2, with randomized single- and multiple-mask trials rather than blocked, the consistent cueing effects found in E1 were generally supported. Importantly, regardless of speed versus accuracy emphasis, we found robust cueing effects in the single-mask condition in both RT and accuracy. Whereas our results support signal enhancement as one mechanism of cueing effects, we acknowledge that multiple mechanisms may be operating to affect performance in a Posner-style cueing paradigm. OPEN PRACTICES STATEMENT: The studies presented here were preregistered on the Open Science Framework (OSF). The preregistrations, raw (trial-level) data from both experiments, experimental code, and analysis script can all be found can be found at: https://osf.io/2dcvj/.

papers.title: More Than the Visual Cortex, Age‐Related Differences in Representational Momentum Stem From Network Reorganization: Insights From Dynamic Functional Connectivity
papers.authors: Guangfang Zhou, Juntao Chen, Xiaokang Jin et al.
papers.summary: Older adults tend to misjudge where a moving target stops by pushing the estimate further along its direction of motion, which is called representational momentum. Here, resting-state fMRI and whole-brain dynamic connectivity analysis showed that older adults had larger forward displacement, were less flexible in switching brain states, and spent longer in a weakly connected state. Changes in these connectivity measures partly mediated the link between age and displacement, suggesting the effect reflects wider network reorganization and not just visual cortex decline.
papers.abstract: When estimating the final location of moving targets, the individual's judgment tends to exhibit a systematic forward displacement along the direction of motion, a phenomenon termed representational momentum (RM). The age effect on RM has been a focus of research, and a recent study reports an age‐related increase in forward displacement among older adults, potentially linked to functional decline in the visual cortex. However, this study exclusively focused on the visual cortex, thereby limiting a comprehensive understanding of the neural mechanisms underlying age‐related differences in RM. To address this limitation, the neural basis of age‐related differences in RM was investigated for the first time by combining resting‐state functional magnetic resonance imaging with whole‐brain dynamic functional connectivity (dFC) analysis. The results revealed a significant increase in forward displacement among older adults compared with younger adults, particularly when targets moved from left to right. Neuroimaging data revealed reduced flexibility in transitioning between brain states and prolonged dwell time in the “weak state” characterized by weak and sparse connectivity, in older adults compared to younger adults. Moreover, within this “weak state,” attenuated intranetwork connectivity and increased internetwork connectivity were observed in the aging brain. Critically, alterations in these dFC metrics partially mediated the relationship between age and forward displacement. These findings are discussed within the framework of computational theory and the dedifferentiation and compensation hypothesis of brain aging.

papers.title: Vision-Language Models Reproduce a Human Mental-Extrapolation Bias in the Watanabe Illusion
papers.authors: Eiji Watanabe, Kyohei Ueda, Kagayaki Kato et al.
papers.summary: The Watanabe Illusion is one where a line geometrically points at the top dot in a column, yet humans (n = 131) report a dot near the middle. Five vision-language models gave the same biased answers. In Qwen2.5-VL-32B, the vision encoder carried the correct information and the right answer showed up in middle language layers, only to be overwritten in late layers. Prompts naming the illusion or asking for suppression didn't help, and only revealing the answer moved the response, so the bias seems to arise at the language-generation stage.
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used for visual judgments, yet whether they share human perceptual biases, and where in the model such biases arise, is unclear. We addressed this with the Watanabe Illusion, a stimulus not previously studied quantitatively: an oblique segment inside a circle whose extension geometrically hits the topmost of 11 dots, yet human observers (n = 131) reported a dot near the middle of the column. Five VLMs (Qwen2.5-VL-32B and 7B, Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.5 Instant, Gemini 3.5 Flash), given the identical stimulus and wording, all deviated in the same direction. In the open-weight Qwen2.5-VL-32B, linear probes on the vision encoder recovered the line angle and the target dot six to eight times more accurately than its behavioral responses. A layer-wise logit lens showed that the correct answer dominates in the middle layers of the language model and is overwritten in late layers only under a visual-judgment frame. Naming the illusion, requesting suppression of prior knowledge, forcing a visual chain of thought, and 390 semantic preambles left the response center unchanged; only disclosing the correct answer moved it. VLMs may therefore carry human perceptual biases at the language-generation stage, where they resist declarative correction.

papers.title: Random Exploration is Random
papers.authors: Yingkang Luo, Hua-Dong Xiong, Hanbo Xie et al.
papers.summary: Random exploration is the idea that people choose more variably when exploring, and this work asks whether that variability is truly random or just structure that standard models miss. Using the Horizon Task data from 1,392 participants, the researchers fit neural networks that were more flexible than traditional models. The networks predicted behavior better overall, yet long-horizon choices stayed consistently less predictable than short-horizon ones, suggesting that the extra variability really is largely random.
papers.abstract: Decision making often requires balancing exploitation of familiar options with exploration of uncertain alternatives. One strategy for exploration is random exploration, in which choices become more variable and less tied to the option that currently appears best. However, it remains unclear whether this variability reflects genuine stochasticity or instead a deterministic structure that traditional cognitive models fail to capture. We examined this question using the Horizon Task in an aggregated dataset of 1,392 participants completing over 1,270,695 trials. In this task, exploration becomes more valuable when participants have more future choices, and choice variability increases under longer horizons. We tested whether more expressive neural network models could recover deterministic structure from this additional variability. Although neural networks provided better overall fits to behavior than the traditional model, long-horizon choices remained consistently less predictable than short-horizon choices. These findings show that limited model expressiveness cannot fully account for the increased variability associated with random exploration, suggesting random exploration truly is substantially random.

papers.title: MuSeToM: Multi-Sensory Evaluation of Belief Revision with Textual Cues Across Six Senses
papers.authors: Chunkit Chan, Kawai Chung, Sze Heng Douglas Kwok et al.
papers.summary: MuSeToM is a text-based benchmark of 2,415 items, adapted from BigToM and OpenToM, that tests whether language models can tell when perceptual evidence across six senses justifies someone revising a belief. Evaluating current LLMs with direct and chain-of-thought prompting, the researchers found they often notice that a belief might change but struggle to work out the new belief. They also tend to over-update on cues that are salient but not actually sufficient evidence.
papers.abstract: Theory of Mind (ToM), the ability to infer mental states in others, is pivotal for human social cognition. Existing evaluations of ToM in large language models (LLMs) mainly focus on static belief attribution and false-belief reasoning, leaving a critical aspect of social reasoning underexplored: can LLMs decide whether perceptual evidence is sufficient to justify another person's belief revision? To address this gap, we present MuSeToM, a human-validated, text-based benchmark for evaluating epistemic belief revision in ToM reasoning. MuSeToM contains 2,415 instances adapted from BigToM and OpenToM, with textual cues spanning six sensory categories, and tests whether models can determine when a protagonist should revise a belief and infer the resulting updated belief state. Using MuSeToM, we systematically evaluate state-of-the-art LLMs under direct and chain-of-thought prompting, revealing a pronounced dissonance: while models often detect that a belief may change, they struggle to identify the updated belief and frequently over-update on perceptually salient but epistemically insufficient cues.

papers.title: Individual differences in vision science: The case for a paradigm shift, what it buys, and how to do it well
papers.authors: David Henry Peterzell
papers.summary: Revisiting a 2017 paper on what individual differences can teach vision science, this piece argues that studying them is a full paradigm that should enter the mainstream, treating differences among observers as evidence rather than error. It centers on latent factors, lays out twelve pillars of what the approach offers, and corrects several 2017 conclusions, including the definition of true individual differences as stable traits and a set of prescriptions such as rank statistics and mandatory blocking. The long-term goal is a computational atlas of human visual variation.
papers.abstract: Nearly a decade ago, Mollon, Bosten, Peterzell, and Webster (2017) asked what individual differences can teach visual science and what counts as good experimental practice. Studies since then have changed both answers. The study of individual differences is a paradigm, not a technique, with its own objects, standards of evidence, and products. Long practiced in the shadows by a small group, it should move into the mainstream and integrate with existing paradigms, treating differences among observers as evidence rather than error. Its central object is the latent factor, which can earn roles from latent mechanism to established mechanism, computational phenotype, heritable phenotype, endophenotype, or factor-targeted marker, each requiring stricter evidence. Twelve pillars organize what the paradigm buys, including links across domains and levels and tests of whether constructs are unitary. Several 2017 conclusions need correction, above all the definition of true individual differences as stable, long-term traits, and the 2017 prescriptions (rank statistics, required test-retest reliability, fixed test order, mandatory blocking, blanket correction for multiple comparisons) each trade one error for another. Because global artifacts produce general factors, tuned factor structure is itself evidence against them. The long-term goal is a computational atlas of human visual variation: its mechanisms, their sources, and optimal markers for the clinic and for design.

papers.title: Developing human-AI complementarity: Augmenting everyday decision making with Large Language Models
papers.authors: Adrian Paul Banks, David M Gamblin
papers.summary: Across three longitudinal studies (N = 671), people described a real two-option decision and reported how it turned out a week later. An LLM supplied considerations tailored to each decision, and participants chose which to keep, so the final judgment stayed theirs. Evaluations built this way predicted outcomes best in all three studies, and in Study 2 the fully augmented version beat both the human-only and AI-only evaluations and explained extra variance beyond the two combined. That makes it a concrete case of human-AI complementarity, which is rarely found.
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) can improve human judgement, but human–AI systems rarely achieve complementarity: combined performance exceeding that of both humans and AI alone. Across three longitudinal studies (N = 671), we tested whether large language models (LLMs) could support complementarity by contributing to the construction and revision of everyday decision representations. Participants reported real, personally meaningful decisions involving two options and the decision outcome success one week later. As decisions were participant-generated rather than predefined, LLMs dynamically generated considerations and alternative evaluations tailored to each decision. We compared the predictive validity of AI, Human, and augmented evaluations. AI evaluations were standalone LLM predictions of decision outcome success. Human weighted-additive evaluations combined participant-generated attributes, importance weights, and option ratings. Augmented evaluations incorporated LLM-generated attributes and, in later studies, suggested weights and ratings, while participants selected attributes and retained control over evaluations. Augmented evaluations consistently predicted experienced outcomes and showed the strongest observed associations across all three studies. Evidence for complementarity was clearest in Study 2, where fully augmented evaluations outperformed both standalone approaches and explained additional variance in expected and experienced outcomes beyond the standalone evaluations considered together. Across studies, augmentation expanded the attribute set, with participants retaining human and AI contributions. These findings show that human–AI complementarity can emerge in predicting success of real decision outcomes and suggest that decision architecture matters. A distributed cognitive system that integrates AI contributions across all stages of decision making while humans remain responsible for selection and judgement of personally relevant considerations offers a promising architecture for evaluating diverse, personally meaningful real-life decisions.

papers.title: Perceptual distinctiveness underlies apparent emotion-specific advantages in facial expression detection
papers.authors: Erika Bucci, Giacomo Handjaras, Giada Lettieri et al.
papers.summary: Faster detection of happy and angry faces is usually read as evidence that we prioritize emotion. These researchers ran preregistered visual search experiments, geometric modeling of expressions, and eye tracking, and found the advantage showed up only when expression intensity wasn't balanced. With intensity matched, equivalence tests found no practically meaningful effect of emotion. Detection was best predicted by how far a face deviated geometrically from neutral, whatever the emotion, which challenges the evolutionary story.
papers.abstract: Humans are assumed to prioritize facial expressions because of the evolutionary significance of their affective content. Here, we show that this assumption does not survive rigorous control of perceptual structure. Across three studies integrating preregistered visual search experiments, geometric modeling of facial expressions, and eye-tracking data, we tested whether detection advantages for happy and angry faces reflect low-level visual salience rather than emotion. To this end, we combined frequentist interval testing with a predefined smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) and Bayesian region-of-practical-equivalence (ROPE) analyses. Behavioral and oculomotor measures reliably predicted emotion category when expressions were presented at full, perceptually unbalanced intensity. By contrast, when expression intensity was matched, both interval testing and Bayesian ROPE analyses supported the absence of a practically meaningful effect. In addition, detection speed and accuracy were best explained by geometric deviation from a neutral face, independent of emotional category. These findings indicate that apparent emotion advantages in visual search arise from perceptual salience rather than privileged access to emotion, challenging evolutionary accounts of attentional prioritization.

papers.title: From the app to the lexicon: Neurocognitive markers of word integration in a second language
papers.authors: Ramón Igarreta, Luz Bavassi, Laura Kaczer
papers.summary: Native Spanish speakers learned Guarani on Duolingo for five weeks, then did a semantic decision task while EEG was recorded. Words learned early in training (remote) showed a clear N400 priming effect, the brain's sign of semantic relatedness, but words learned in the final stage (recent, tested about 10 days later) showed none. Accuracy for related words also favored remote over recent items. Together this suggests consolidation time matters for integrating app-learned words into semantic memory, and it's a nice pairing of real-world learning with controlled neural testing.
papers.abstract: The consolidation of newly learned vocabulary into semantic memory networks is a critical process in word learning, including second-language (L2) acquisition. However, most neurocognitive studies of lexical-semantic integration rely on short, artificial learning paradigms, leaving open the question of whether naturalistic, app-based learning produces comparable neural outcomes. In this study, we combined an ecological learning environment with controlled electrophysiological testing to examine whether vocabulary learned through Duolingo shows neural signatures of semantic integration. Native Spanish speakers studied Guarani vocabulary for five weeks and subsequently completed a semantic decision task during EEG recording that included both L1 (Spanish) and L2 (Guarani) word pairs. Critically, L2 targets were classified as remote (learned earlier during the five-week training and not practiced in the final stage) or recent (learned in the final training stage and tested approximately 10 days later), allowing us to assess consolidation-related differences. Behaviorally, participants responded more accurately and faster to L1 than L2 words, and accuracy for related items was higher for remotely than recently learned items, consistent with consolidation-related strengthening. Electrophysiologically, robust N400 priming effects emerged for remotely learned words—whereas no facilitation was observed for recent words. This graded pattern suggests that only words with extended consolidation time exhibited neural markers of lexical–semantic integration. Together, these findings demonstrate that combining real-world digital learning with controlled neural testing can reveal how naturalistic language experience shapes the neurocognitive dynamics of word learning and consolidation.

papers.title: Auditory category learning in children with dyslexia
papers.authors: Casey L Roark, Vishal J Thakkar, Bharath Chandrasekaran et al.
papers.summary: Children aged 7-12 with dyslexia (n = 25) and typically developing peers (n = 25) learned auditory categories. The dyslexic children showed a deficit in rule-based category learning, the declarative, hypothesis-testing kind. That's the opposite of adults with dyslexia, who in earlier work struggled with information-integration learning but not rule-based learning. The authors suggest people with dyslexia may develop compensatory strategies that protect declarative learning over development while procedural difficulties remain.
papers.abstract: Purpose: Developmental dyslexia is proposed to involve selective procedural memory deficits with intact declarative memory. Recent research in the domain of category learning has demonstrated that adults with dyslexia have selective deficits in information-integration category learning that is proposed to rely on procedural learning mechanisms and unaffected rule-based category learning that is proposed to rely on declarative, hypothesis testing mechanisms. Importantly, learning mechanisms also change across development, with distinct developmental trajectories in both procedural and declarative learning mechanisms. It is unclear how dyslexia in childhood should influence auditory category learning, a critical skill for speech perception and reading development. Method: We examined auditory category learning performance and strategies in 7-12-year-old children with dyslexia (n = 25, 9 Females, 16 Males) and typically developing controls (n = 25, 13 Females, 12 Males). Results: We found that children with dyslexia have a rule-based category learning deficit, rather than the selective information-integration learning deficit observed in prior work in adults with dyslexia. Conclusions: These results suggest that the important skill of auditory category learning is impacted in children with dyslexia and throughout development, individuals with dyslexia may develop compensatory strategies that preserve declarative learning while developing difficulties in procedural learning.

papers.title: When actions speak louder than words: Contributions of action imagery and verbal rehearsal to maintaining verbally instructed movement representations
papers.authors: Carla Czilczer, Markus Martini, Pierre Sachse et al.
papers.summary: When you imagine a sequence of movements from spoken instructions, what holds that evolving image in mind? Participants imagined three to six movements and judged whether a figure matched the final position, sometimes while repeating a syllable aloud to block verbal rehearsal. Suppression increased errors, but performance stayed above chance. Errors tracked visuospatial rather than verbal working memory, and most people reported visually rehearsing the instructed body parts. So maintenance seems to rest mainly on visual rehearsal and visuospatial working memory, with verbal rehearsal helping out, and the task may be a useful measure of action imagery ability.
papers.abstract: When imagining actions based on verbal movement instructions, maintaining an evolving mental representation across successive instructions is important. We examined this process from a working memory perspective, asking whether maintenance of verbally instructed action imagery depends on verbal working memory or can be sustained by action imagery-related processes. In an adapted Final Position Judgment Task (FPJT), participants imagined three to six successive movements from listening to standardized movement instructions. They then judged whether an image of a human figure matched their imagined final position. Participants completed the FPJT in two conditions, once in baseline and once while repeating a syllable aloud to prevent verbal rehearsal. This articulatory suppression increased errors but performance remained above chance, suggesting that performance was not reducible to verbal rehearsal. Converging with this, FPJT errors were associated with visuospatial, but not verbal, working memory, with these associations not varying by FPJT condition. Articulatory suppression reduced reported verbal rehearsal and action imagery quality, whereas in both conditions, more than 80% reported visual rehearsal of instructed body parts to maintain imagery. Visual rehearsal was associated with fewer errors in baseline. Our results suggest that maintaining verbally instructed action imagery in the FPJT relies on action imagery-related visual rehearsal and visuospatial working memory, with verbal rehearsal playing a supporting role. Given that FPJT performance also covaried with mental body rotation and mental paper folding performance, the FPJT appears suitable for assessing action imagery ability.

papers.title: Neural evidence for intact statistical learning in Developmental Dyslexia in the absence of conclusive behavioral results: an individual differences approach to cognitive correlates
papers.authors: Iris Maria van der Wulp, Marijn Eefje Struiksma, Frank Wijnen
papers.summary: Adults with self-reported dyslexia (n = 25) and typical readers (n = 118) listened to an artificial language while EEG tracked neural entrainment to the nonsense words, a measure of statistical learning. Both groups showed neural evidence of learning, with similar entrainment. Behavioral scores looked lower in the dyslexia group, but Bayesian analyses were inconclusive. The dyslexia group did score lower on rhythm, working memory and vocabulary, mostly the latter two, and links between these and neural learning didn't differ by group. The authors argue for studying individual differences rather than only comparing groups.
papers.abstract: Individual differences in Statistical Learning (SL) are associated with reading ability, yet evidence on whether SL is impaired in Developmental Dyslexia (DD) is inconsistent. Furthermore, DD is associated with impairments in Rhythmic Ability (RA) and Working Memory (WM). This study examined SL in adults with self-reported diagnoses of DD compared to Typical Readers (TR), and explored whether individual differences in RA, WM, and vocabulary related to individual SL ability in speech segmentation.A total of 143 participants (N_DD = 25, N_TR = 118) were exposed to an artificial language of trisyllabic nonsense-words while neural entrainment to the words assessed SL via electroencephalography (EEG), followed by behavioral SL outcome measures. Aiming to assess individual differences, we linked the neural measure of SL to a battery of tests measuring musicality, RA, WM, and vocabulary size. Results indicated neural evidence for SL in both groups, with similar neural entrainment to the structure during exposure. Behavioral performance in the DD group on SL seemed below TR, though Bayesian analyses rendered this inconclusive. The DD group obtained lower scores on tasks measuring RA, WM and vocabulary size, which was primarily driven by the latter two. Comparison of relations between neural SL and these tasks indicated no group differences therein. Exploratively combining the groups into one population resulted in anecdotal Bayesian evidence that individual differences in SL related to WM and RA measured by sensorimotor synchronization, which was rendered inconclusive in sensitivity analyses. Our results emphasize the importance of an individual differences approach, moving beyond group comparisons.

papers.title: Language enables cumulative cultural improvement by transmitting mental models
papers.authors: Alexandre Bluet, Shen Tian, David Schultner et al.
papers.summary: Some knowledge, like why something works, can't easily be read off successful behavior. In a ten-generation transmission chain (N = 2,000) using a task with a hidden relational structure, participants either watched the previous person's behavior or read their written advice. Observation produced no cumulative gains, while written advice led to steady improvements in performance and task knowledge. Messages got better over generations, increasingly conveying the hidden structure and dropping incorrect or irrelevant content. This points to language as a way of passing on mental models in cumulative culture.
papers.abstract: Human culture is distinguished by the accumulation of increasingly sophisticated knowledge of why things work, much of which cannot be readily recovered from observing successful behavior alone. How such knowledge is transmitted across generations remains poorly understood. We tested whether cumulative improvement depends on how knowledge is shared using a decision-making task governed by a hidden relational structure that could not be reliably inferred from observed behavior. Across ten sequential generations (N = 2,000), participants solved the task after either observing a previous participant's behavior or receiving their written advice. Observation produced no cumulative gains, whereas language yielded sustained intergenerational improvements in performance and task knowledge. Messages were progressively refined, increasingly communicating the hidden task structure while filtering incorrect and task-irrelevant content. These findings suggest that language may support cumulative culture when the mental models underlying successful behavior cannot be readily recovered through observation alone.

papers.title: Longitudinal and cross-sectional perspectives on elementary school children's post-error slowing in reading and arithmetic
papers.authors: Claudia M Roebers, Daniela Menath, Hülya Özmen et al.
papers.summary: Children in 2nd and 4th grade (N = 622) did tablet-based arithmetic and word-reading tasks twice over six months. Both grades slowed down after errors in both domains, a sign they were monitoring and adjusting. The slowing was bigger in arithmetic than in reading, bigger in 4th graders, and grew over time. It also helped accuracy afterward in arithmetic, especially for younger children, but not in reading, so error monitoring seems to work differently across academic domains.
papers.abstract: This study investigated the development of primary school children’s error-related adjustments in reading and arithmetic. N = 622 children from 2nd and 4th grade were tested on two tablet-based academic tasks twice in six months: an arithmetic task composed of addition and doubling items with two answer options and a silent word reading task matching words with four pictorial answer options. Children in both grades showed robust post-error slowing (PES) in both reading and arithmetic, indicating reliable monitoring and strategy use in the form of upregulating cognitive control mechanisms. Overall, post-error slowing was larger in arithmetic than in reading, independent of grade and measurement point. Fourth graders showed larger PES than 2nd graders, especially at T1, and both grades’ PES increased from T1 to T2, suggesting that task experience, improving monitoring skills, and strategy discovery play an important role. In terms of the benefits of PES for performance accuracy, PES was linked to better accuracy after the error in the arithmetic task, particularly for younger children. This was not the case for reading. Results are discussed in terms of often overlooked educationally relevant strategies in arithmetic, possible strategy’s utilization deficiency, developing monitoring and cognitive control skills in this age range and differing processing demands across academic domains.

papers.title: Some Assembly Required: Self-Testing Alone is Not an Effective Way to Build Broader Understanding
papers.authors: Benjamin Motz, Anna Chinni, Audrey Barriball et al.
papers.summary: Self-testing is known to boost memory for tested facts, but does it help you connect ideas? In two experiments (n = 254, plus a preregistered replication with a 24-hour delay, n = 68), self-testing improved fact recall but gave worse inference performance than self-explanation. Generating inferences while learning predicted inference performance, while noting facts predicted fact recall. Participants also produced fewer inferences with science texts than with narratives. Retrieval practice strengthens individual memories, but building coherent understanding seems to need active inference-making.
papers.abstract: Extensive research has demonstrated that testing enhances long-term memory by strengthening retrieval processes for the tested memory traces. Such memory models explain why learners benefit from repeated testing but do not account for how learners construct understanding across multiple ideas. In contrast, theories of discourse comprehension emphasize the construction of inferences, whereby learners actively connect ideas into a coherent mental representation. These two perspectives—memory-based retrieval versus inference-based integration—make distinct predictions about what learners retain and understand. The present study tested these predictions by comparing self-testing, self-explanation, and reading strategies on both fact memory and inference performance. In Experiment 1 (n = 254), despite superior retention of individual facts, self-testing produced lower inference performance than self-explanation. Experiment 2 (n = 68), a preregistered replication with a minimum 24-hour delay, confirmed and extended these findings: repeated retrieval improved recall of facts but did not facilitate the assembly of coherent knowledge structures. A mixed-methods analysis revealed that generating inferences during learning specifically predicted inference performance, whereas noting facts predicted fact recall, providing converging evidence that these strategies produce qualitatively different mental representations. Furthermore, participants generated fewer inferences when self-explaining science texts compared with narratives, highlighting domain differences in the ease of knowledge integration. Together, these results demonstrate that while self-testing strengthens memory for discrete information, it fails to foster the integrative processing necessary for comprehension. Effective learning requires more than strengthening retrieval processes—it depends on the active generation of inferences that bind ideas into coherent mental models.

papers.title: A “Human-Like” Stroop Effect No Longer Implies a Human Participant
papers.authors: Talha Özüdoğru, Christian Janssen, Silja Renooij et al.
papers.summary: With AI agents now able to complete online experiments, the researchers compared Stroop data from 51 respondents each: in-person verified humans, an artificial experiment agent, and an online sample. The agent showed the usual congruency effect and passed six quality checks. A one-class SVM trained only on human data reached a median accuracy of 63%. A supervised SVM trained on both reached 94% but failed on an agent it hadn't seen, and at a 5% contamination rate most of its flags would be false alarms. The takeaway is to protect human participation through study design rather than screening afterward.
papers.abstract: Researchers have long assumed that online behavioral experiments are completed by humans, an assumption AI agents can now violate. We asked whether agent and human data can be distinguished. We compared Stroop data from 51 respondents each: humans verified in person, an artificial experiment agent, and an online sample. All agent-generated respondents showed the congruency effect and passed six quality checks. A one-class support vector machine (SVM) trained only on human data achieved a median accuracy of 63%. A supervised SVM trained on human and agent data achieved 94%. At an assumed 5% contamination rate, most of its flags would be false alarms. The supervised SVM did not generalize to an agent it was not trained on. Neither plausible task performance nor the tested SVMs reliably distinguished human from agent data. These findings suggest that human participation should be safeguarded through study design rather than through screening afterward.

papers.title: Acoustic and visual cues to lexical stress interact with semantic predictions in Spanish lexical stress perception
papers.authors: Floris Cos, Matteo Maran, Hans Rutger Bosker et al.
papers.summary: Spanish stress pairs like clasiFIco versus clasifiCÓ were placed in sentences that favored one reading. Stress was varied acoustically, and visually through a beat gesture aligned to different syllables. Listeners picked the matching pronoun. Acoustic cues clearly guided responses and response times, while gesture timing didn't change which pronoun was chosen. Responses were faster, though, when the gesture matched the meaning the sentence context favored, so gesture timing does affect word recognition in full sentences.
papers.abstract: Next to acoustic cues, lexical stress can be communicated visually through the timing of beat gestures. This study investigated for the first time how auditory and visual lexical stress cues are weighted in meaningful sentences. Minimal stress pairs of Spanish verb forms (clasiFIco, “I classify” vs. clasifiCÓ, “(s)he classified”) were embedded in sentence contexts that biased towards either member of the pair. Stress was manipulated acoustically along a continuum, and visually by aligning a beat gesture to the penultimate or last syllable. Native listeners selected the pronoun (yo “I” or ella “she”) they felt fit best with the sentence. Listeners were sensitive to acoustic cues, as indicated by both responses and response times. While gesture alignment did not significantly affect pronoun selection, response times were shorter when the gesture matched the semantic context bias. This study thus shows that in full sentences, congruent (vs. incongruent) gestural timing affects word recognition.

papers.title: Conditional reasoning in preschoolers: The role of context and alternatives
papers.authors: Ebru Evcen, David Barner
papers.summary: School-aged children tend to struggle with the literal reading of conditionals like 'If you eat your broccoli, you'll get a candy', where broccoli is just one way to get candy. In two studies, children as young as 4 reached adult-like literal interpretations when context supported them: either alternatives were made salient (Exp 1), or the antecedent wasn't causally related to the consequent (Exp 2). This suggests preschoolers have the logical ability and processing resources for conditional inference when given contextual support.
papers.abstract: Understanding conditional inferences is fundamental to human reasoning, allowing us to evaluate possibilities and predict outcomes. For instance, the conditional, “If you eat your broccoli, you’ll get a candy” can be interpreted literally, meaning eating broccoli is one way to get a candy, or pragmatically, implying it is the only way. Past studies find school-aged children (ages 7-12) struggle to arrive at literal meanings but, interestingly, compute adult-like, pragmatic interpretations at this age. An important limitation of past research is the lack of testing in contexts that support literal meanings. We conducted two studies to examine whether children can derive literal interpretations when supported by context. We found that preschoolers as young as 4 years old are adult-like in computing literal meanings when they are able to judge that the antecedent is not the only way to bring about the consequent, either because discourse introduces salient alternatives (Exp 1) or because the stated antecedent is not causally related to the consequent (Exp 2). These findings suggest that preschoolers have the logical ability and processing resources required to make conditional inferences when provided with contextual support.

papers.title: Effects of active learning and talker variability on preschoolers' novel word learning
papers.authors: Federica Bulgarelli, Marina Rabideau
papers.summary: Instead of passively hearing words from assigned talkers, preschoolers could choose who to hear novel words from. They chose to hear words from multiple talkers. Talker variability choices interacted with active learning to predict word production but not comprehension. So young children can make choices that benefit their own learning, which informs theories of both talker variability and active learning.
papers.abstract: Words sound different every time they are said, both by the same person and across people. This variability has been found to have mixed effects on learning. For example, 14-month-olds benefit from talker variability when learning minimal pairs, but struggle when learning distinct-sounding words. Talker variability is found to be particularly beneficial for learning to produce novel words. All of these previous studies have used passive exposure, presenting participants with predetermined orders or fixed types of variability. Here, we used an active learning paradigm wherein preschoolers could choose who to hear words from during word learning. Then, we tested whether participants seek out variability during word learning, how these talker variability choices influence word learning and whether actively making these choices results in different outcomes than passively receiving them. We find that preschoolers choose to hear words from multiple talkers, and talker variability choices interact with active learning to predict production, but not comprehension. Taken together, our results suggest that preschool aged children can make choices are benefit their own learning, informing theories of both talker variability and active learning.

papers.title: Keep It in Sight: Reward Function Compression Through Goal Visibility
papers.authors: Xitong Chen, Chaofan Li, Gaia Molinaro et al.
papers.summary: Learning from abstract goals is usually slower than learning from explicit points. The reward function compression hypothesis says this is because evaluating goal outcomes taxes limited resources, though the cost shrinks as people learn an efficient evaluation rule. A rival account says it's just an immediate dual-task cost of holding the goal in mind. In an experiment with 61 participants, visible goals gradually reduced the learning cost, eventually approaching point-based performance, while visible non-goals helped much less. That fits compression and not simple memory offloading. Modeling linked faster outcome evaluation to better learning rather than to decision noise.
papers.abstract: Humans often learn from outcomes defined by abstract goals rather than explicit rewards. This flexibility supports real-world behavior but typically causes slower and less efficient learning compared to directly observable rewards. We asked where the cognitive bottleneck arises as abstract goals are transformed into learning signals. The reward function compression hypothesis proposes that this inefficiency arises because evaluating abstract goal outcomes burdens limited cognitive resources otherwise directed toward learning, and that this cognitive cost can decrease over iterations when a specialized, efficient goal-dependent outcome evaluation function is learned. Alternatively, this cost could simply arise from an immediate dual-task effect, where goal maintenance imposes a cost on decisions.To distinguish these two hypotheses, we manipulated the visibility of goal and non-goal information throughout learning and feedback. While the memory-offloading account predicts that this manipulation should immediately rescue goal-based learning, the reward function compression hypothesis predicts a gradually acquired benefit proportional to the compressibility of the match/mismatch rule. Our results (N = 61) supported the reward compression hypothesis. Visible goals gradually reduced learning efficiency costs, eventually approaching the point-based learning performance. An equivalent decrease in memory load (visible non-goals) did not boost learning as much, highlighting the role of outcome evaluation in goal-directed learning. Computational modeling revealed that outcome evaluation efficiency, proxied by participants' ``reward collection'' response time, specifically influenced participants' learning processes, rather than decision noise. These results show that learning from goals depends on our ability to train efficient estimators of outcome values, which is facilitated by keeping goals in sight.

papers.title: Reading Minds Beyond the Eyes: Conceptual Knowledge Structures Mental State Perception
papers.authors: Maryam Bin Meshar, Jonathan B. Freeman
papers.summary: Across four studies (N = 827), people identified complex mental states more accurately from full faces than from faces with the eyes removed or from the eyes alone, so information beyond the eyes matters. States people believed tend to co-occur looked more similar in facial appearance and were more often confused with each other, for both posed and naturalistic faces. Each person's idiosyncratic conceptual associations predicted their own similarity judgments and their specific misidentifications, even beyond associations shared across people. So differences in conceptual knowledge may explain why people read the same face differently.
papers.abstract: The ability to infer others’ mental states is central to understanding human behavior. Across four studies (total N = 827), we examined how facial information and perceivers’ conceptual knowledge structure mental-state inferences. In Study 1, participants identified 60 complex mental states more accurately from full faces than from faces with the eye region removed or isolated eye regions, demonstrating the importance of information beyond the eyes. Study 2 showed that mental states believed to co-occur were perceived as more similar in facial appearance. Crucially, perceivers’ idiosyncratic conceptual associations predicted their own facial-similarity judgments even after accounting for associations shared across participants. Studies 3 and 4 extended this correspondence from perceptual similarity to categorical identification: conceptually associated states were more likely to be confused with one another, both for standardized posed expressions and for naturalistic, unposed faces. On trials involving misidentification, participants’ unique conceptual associations predicted which incorrect mental-state label they selected above and beyond shared conceptual structure. Together, these findings suggest that inferring mental states from faces depends on both distributed facial information and the conceptual organization perceivers bring to the task. More broadly, they identify individual differences in conceptual knowledge as a source of systematic variation in how people read minds from the same facial expressions.
